known_from: ch02-term-registry.json (terms defined there count as known in every chapter)

terms.definition: a small, famous table of 150 flowers: 4 measurements per flower (petal and sepal length and width, in cm) plus the flower's species. It ships inside Scikit-Learn.
the coloured leaf-like parts of a flower. The iris data measures each flower's petal length and petal width in centimetres.
the kind of iris a flower is: setosa, versicolor or virginica. It is the label the iris model learns to predict.

one of the categories a classifier chooses between; here a species (class 0 = setosa, 1 = versicolor, 2 = virginica). Careful: Python also says "class" for a blueprint that objects are made from, such as `DecisionTreeClassifier`. Which one is meant is always clear from the sentence.
a model that predicts a class (a category), such as a species, rather than a number.
a task where the model must produce several answers per row at once (for example two numbers), not just one.
Classification And Regression Tree: the recipe Scikit-Learn uses to grow a decision tree. b04 explains it step by step.
the hyperparameter that caps how many questions deep a tree may grow. max_depth=2 means at most two questions from the top to an answer.
how many questions below the top a node sits: the top node is depth 0, its two children are depth 1, and so on.
a free program that turns a plain-text description of boxes and arrows (a `.dot` file) into a picture. `export_graphviz()` is the Scikit-Learn function that writes that text for a trained tree.
one box of the tree. Each node either asks a yes/no question or, at the bottom, gives the answer.
the top node of the tree, where every walk starts (depth 0).
a node at the bottom with no question of its own: it only holds the answer for every row that reaches it.
a node that still asks a yes/no question and sends each row left (yes) or right (no).
a node directly below another one; every split node has exactly two, a left child and a right child.
one yes/no question of a tree, such as "is petal length at most 2.45 cm?", which divides the rows at a node into two groups.
the number a split compares a feature against, such as the 2.45 in "petal length at most 2.45 cm".
a score from 0 to below 1 for how mixed the classes are at a node: 0 means every row there is the same class; higher means more mixed. Equation 6-1 shows how it is computed.
how mixed the classes are in a group of rows. A group of one class only is "pure" (impurity 0).
a node or group whose rows all belong to one class; its impurity is 0.
the number printed on a node: how many training rows reached that node.
the list printed on a node: how many of the rows at that node belong to each class, e.g. [0, 49, 5].
a tree whose every question has exactly two answers (yes/no), so every split node has exactly two children.
an older tree-growing recipe, not in Scikit-Learn, that can split a node into more than two branches.
a model whose reasoning you can read and check by hand, like a small decision tree.
a large model built from many layers of simple calculations; very accurate on images and text, but not readable by hand. Chapter 10 starts on them.
the field of methods for explaining why a model made a prediction.
a number from 0 to 1 (0% to 100%) for how likely something is. `predict_proba()` returns one probability per class.
a function that stays flat across a whole range and then jumps, like a staircase, instead of changing smoothly.
the line (or edge) in the picture of the data where the model's answer changes from one class to another.
a model for classification (despite its name) that turns the features into a smooth probability; the book's Chapter 4 covers it.
a search that takes the best-looking option at each step and never goes back to reconsider it.
the one number a training algorithm tries to make as small as possible; for CART it is the size-weighted impurity of a split (Equation 6-2).
an average where bigger groups count more: each group's number is multiplied by its share of the rows before adding up.
a family of problems for which no fast method is known: the only known guaranteed method tries so many options that the time grows explosively (exponentially) with the input size.
growth that multiplies instead of adding: each extra row multiplies the work, so it gets out of hand very fast.
a hyperparameter: every leaf must hold at least this many training rows, so the tree cannot carve out a leaf for one odd row.
a hyperparameter: a node needs at least this many rows before it is allowed to split.
a hyperparameter: the tree may have at most this many leaves.
a hyperparameter: how many features are tried at each split (all of them, by default).
the same rule as min_samples_leaf, written as a share of all training rows instead of a count.
log₂(m) = how many times you can halve m before reaching 1. log₂(8) = 3 because 8 → 4 → 2 → 1; log₂(150) ≈ 7.2.
a tree whose leaves all sit at about the same depth, so no path from the top to a leaf is much longer than the others.
how the running time grows as the data grows. "O(m × log₂(m))" reads "grows like m times log₂ of m"; the letter O just means "roughly proportional to".
a second measure of how mixed the classes at a node are: 0 when all rows are one class, larger when mixed. b05 explains where it comes from and compares it with Gini impurity.
the mathematics of messages and surprise, founded by Claude Shannon in 1948; it measures information in bits.
the branch of physics about heat and disorder in matter, where the word entropy was first used.
the unit of information: the amount carried by the answer to one fair yes/no question.
the hyperparameter that picks the impurity measure a tree uses: "gini" (the default) or "entropy".
a model whose number of learned numbers is fixed before training, e.g. a straight line always has one slope per feature plus one intercept.
a model whose number of learned numbers is NOT fixed in advance; it grows with the data, as a tree's number of nodes does.
growing a tree fully, then cutting back the branches that do not earn their place.
a standard statistics test for whether a pattern in counts could plausibly be chance.
a made-up two-feature dataset from Scikit-Learn's `make_moons()`: two interlocking crescent shapes, one per class, with some random scatter (noise).
the share of rows a classifier gets right: 0.92 means 92 rows out of 100.
`model.score(X, y)` predicts every row of X and compares with y; for a classifier it returns the accuracy.
MSE: take each row's miss (prediction minus the true value), square it, then average. It is RMSE before the square root.
a decision tree that predicts a number: each leaf holds the average target of its training rows.
predict for inputs outside the range the model was trained on.
at a right angle. A tree's cuts are perpendicular to one axis: straight up-and-down or straight across in a plot, never diagonal.
one direction of a plot, one per feature; with petal length across and petal width up there are two axes.
two classes that one straight line (or flat plane) can separate completely.
PCA: a method that finds new axes pointing along the directions in which the data spreads out most, and re-writes every row on those axes. The book's Chapter 8 covers it.
turning the whole cloud of points around the middle, without stretching it; distances between points stay the same.
a new column computed from existing ones, e.g. 0.707 × length + 0.707 × width.
a weighted sum of columns: each column times a fixed number, then added.
error that comes from the model being too simple, so it is wrong in the same way every time, whatever sample it was trained on.
using random choices while it runs, so two runs can differ unless the seed is fixed.
the argument that fixes the seed of a Scikit-Learn object's random choices, so every run gives the same result.
two options that score exactly the same, so something else (here a random choice) must decide between them.
adjusting a model's probabilities so that, among rows given 80%, about 80% really are that class.
a kind of decision tree whose questions test a weighted sum of several features, so its cuts can be diagonal. Scikit-Learn does not have one.
the Scikit-Learn function that cuts a dataset's rows at random into a training part and a test part.
a Scikit-Learn helper that draws many random subsets of the rows, one after another.
combining several models' answers by taking the answer most of them gave.
the value that occurs most often in a list; SciPy's `mode()` returns it.
Scikit-Learn's own way of pruning a grown tree: `ccp_alpha` sets how much each extra leaf must improve the tree to be kept.
a family of models that, unlike PCA, use the labels to find the directions that best separate the classes.
an ensemble that trains many small trees one after another, each new tree fixing the errors the earlier ones still make. Chapter 7 teaches it.
